In the adult rat, alanine is the most effective amino acid substrate for hepatic gluconeogensis, and that the rate of alanine synthesis in skeletal muscle increases in response to the need of the liver for gluconeogenesis.
the liver has a high affinity and capacity for the uptake of alanine and that this uptake is stimulated in starvation and by hormones that increase the rate of gluconeogenesis.
alanine is an important precursor for hepatic gluconeogensis, that alanine is derived from muscle and that muscle alanine production is regulated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the rate of alanine synthesis in skeletal muscle in relation to the rate of hepatic gluconeogenesisis, with particular reference to the effects of insulin and glucagon.
the elucidation of the mechanisms by which alanine synthesis and gluconeogenesis are controlled in skeletal muscle and liver respectively.
the elucidation of the factors which control the rate of gluconeogenesis and the relative contribution of the various gluconeogenic precursers to glucose synthesis by the liver.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rate of hepatic glucose production is regulated by the rate of supply of alanine from peripheral tissues.
the liver has an increased capacity to utilize alanine for gluconeogenesis under conditions of enhanced gluconeogenic activity and that alanine is quantitatively a major gluconeogenic substrate.
alanine is quantitatively and qualitatively the most important amino acid for glucose formation in the liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
alanine is quantitatively a very important substrate for gluconeogenic pathways in the liver.
the liver has the ability to synthesize alanine from glucose, to release alanine into the circulation and to re-utilize the alanine for hepatic gluconeogensis.
in vivo, in the fed state, the contribution of alanine to total hepatic gluconeogenesisis small, but in the starved state it becomes quantitatively the major precursor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver is the major site of alanine metabolism in the body.
the liver is a major site of glucose synthesis from alanine.
alanine synthesis in skeletal muscle is a major determinant of the rate of gluconeogenesis in liver.
